events.arc: Single email: name the reader's question about understanding trial signups, show the one concrete first step (a signup goal), say what the dashboard then breaks out (sources, entry pages, conversion rate), answer the 'does this need code' hesitation, and send them to the official guide to set it up or review how theirs is configured.

emails.job: Introduce Plausible and get the reader to open the goal-conversions guide to set up or review a trial-signup goal.
emails.single_idea: If you define your trial signup as a goal in Plausible, the dashboard stops showing one signup total and starts showing which sources and landing pages drive those signups.
emails.objection: Setting up conversion tracking sounds like it means touching my site's code.
must_not_say: any measured lift, percentage improvement, or before/after conversion figures (E5, E6, E7-E12, E11) — the request forbids presuming a measured lift
the reader's current analytics tool or any Google Analytics comparison or import
any specific traffic volume or pageview tier (do not presume their scale)
privacy, cookieless, GDPR/CCPA or EU-hosting claims — the request forbids presuming their compliance status
funnels, user journeys, revenue attribution and other paid-tier features not needed for the first step

Plausible can only record a paid conversion if the owner sends it as a backend event, revenue attribution sits on the Business plan, and the ledger contains nothing about in-trial product usage or billing, so the measurement stops at.

The 2.65% to 4.80% lift (E11) came from Plausible editing its own homepage, not from installing Plausible; the product locates entry pages and drop-off steps and the owner still has to make the change and re-measure.
emails.felt_need: Free-trial signups do not convert to paid at a rate the owner considers acceptable, even after a signup surge.
emails.status_quo: They add free trials that require a payment method upfront to try to convert website visitors into paying customers.
emails.why_it_fails: One aggregate number has no breakdown by source or entry page, so every improvement to the signup flow is a guess that can't be attributed to anything.
emails.mechanism: You mark the trial registration as a goal — a pageview goal on the registration or confirmation page needs no code changes because pageviews are collected automatically — and once it's recording, that goal reports its conversion rate alongside the referrer sources and the entry pages that drive conversions.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide how to set up a new trial-signup goal, or review how an existing one is configured, including whether a no-code pageview goal fits your registration flow.
emails.next_step_value: The guide shows that marking your signup as a goal lets the dashboard report its conversion rate plus the referrer sources and entry pages driving conversions, and that pageview goals require no code changes.
emails.next_step_limit: The guide explains how goals work; it doesn't set one up for you or show your own data. Seeing your own sources and landing pages requires Plausible running on your site, and a goal shows data only once it's recording conversions.

Email 1, draft 1: "Which pages drive your trial signups?"
events.subject: Which pages drive your trial signups?
events.preview_text: The sources and landing pages behind each signup, not just the total.
events.body:
You can see **which sources and landing pages** turn visitors into trial signups — not just how many signed up.

Understanding trial signups usually means watching one number: the total that registered. On its own, that total can't tell you which referrer or entry page brought them, so every change to your signup flow is a guess.

Plausible is a web analytics dashboard. You mark your trial registration as a goal, and once that goal is recording, the dashboard breaks those signups down by the referrer sources and entry pages driving them.

Setting that up needn't mean touching your site's code. A pageview goal on your registration or confirmation page works because pageviews are collected automatically.

The official goal-conversions guide explains how goals work, so you can decide how to set up a new trial-signup goal or review one you already have. Your own sources show once Plausible is running and the goal starts recording.

events.message: Email 1, draft 1: "Is that signup spike real?"
events.subject: Is that signup spike real?
events.preview_text: A raw count can't tell you — a goal measured against filtered visits can.
events.body:
After a signup burst, the number you judge it by is the raw total.

That total counts whatever reached the page — bots, referrer spam and data-center traffic included. So the conversion rate you work out from it may not reflect real people.

Plausible is a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard. It excludes bots, referrer spam and data-center traffic out of the box, so the visits it counts are real human ones.

Set your trial signup as a goal, and the dashboard reports that goal's conversion rate against those filtered visits — along with the referrer sources and entry pages driving each signup. **One total becomes a breakdown of where real signups come from.**

The official goal-conversions guide walks through setting up a signup goal, or reviewing one you already have. That is the concrete first step before any of it shows up for your own site.
events.postscript: The guide explains how goals work; seeing your own numbers takes Plausible running on your site.

events.preview_text: Set a goal, and one total splits into the sources and pages behind it.
events.body:
A signup burst gives you a bigger number. What it doesn't give you is where that number came from.

A raw count can fold in traffic that was never a person — a visit a conversion rate shouldn't be built on. The total looks the same either way.

Plausible is a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard. It excludes bots, referrer spam and data-center traffic out of the box, so your stats reflect **real human visits**.

Set your trial signup as a goal, and the dashboard reports that goal's conversion rate, the **referrer sources and entry pages** driving it, and the top pages people convert on — all against those filtered visits. One total becomes a breakdown.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through setting up a signup goal, or reviewing one you already have, and shows what each of those breakdowns looks like in the dashboard.
